# Columbia Accident Investigation Board, Report Volume I, Decision-Making Distillation

**Source:** Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003). *Report, Volume I*. August 2003. U.S. Government Printing Office; NASA Technical Reports Server record 20030093634. Licence: **Public domain (US Government work, 17 USC §105; NTRS: "Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted.")**. **Scope:** open. Third-party material inside the report is paraphrased here, never quoted: passages it quotes from outside works (Vaughan, Feynman, Turner, Tufte, the Rogers Commission and earlier review boards), the Boeing slide and figure, and the words of named individuals in quoted e-mails, logs, transcripts and testimony. Every `[V]` below is the Board's own prose, copied from the deep reference.

## Decision-Making Relevance

Chapter 6 of the report is titled "Decision Making at NASA", and it is a close study of a group making a high-stakes decision under uncertainty and getting it wrong in ways that are recognisable well beyond space flight. Managers decided early that a foam strike was not a safety issue, before any analysis had started; an analysis built on a model used far outside its range was presented without its uncertainty; three requests for the information that would have settled the question were turned down; and the decision forum met rarely and heard a three-minute summary (Source: CAIB, *Report Vol. I*, Ch 6, pp. 140–172; Ch 7, p. 192). The Board's analysis supplies decision-makers with a set of tests: who carries the burden of proof, whether the uncertainty reached the deciders, whether a trusted opinion ended the search for others, whether dissent had a route, whether the categories used to label risk had quietly drifted, and whether the schedule was deciding (Ch 6, p. 169; Ch 7, pp. 190–192; Ch 8, pp. 196–203).

It also covers the longer decision cycle. Flight Readiness Reviews ratified known problems as acceptable risks for years, and the Board finds that a process "built on consensus verified by signatures of all responsible parties, in effect renders no one accountable" (Ch 8, p. 198), and that trend analysis, the monitoring that would have shown the drift, was not done (Ch 6, p. 131). It fires in every phase, hardest in Deciding (burden of proof, uncertainty, dissent), Ratifying (consensus-by-signature, rationale reuse) and Monitoring (weak signals, trend analysis, the normalisation of deviance).

## Key Concepts for Decision-Making

1. <!-- concept: inverted-burden-of-proof --> **Who must prove what.** For a hazardous operation the burden should be to prove it safe; NASA asked its engineers to prove it unsafe. "Organizations that deal with high-risk operations must always have a healthy fear of failure — operations must be proved safe, rather than the other way around. NASA inverted this burden of proof." [V] (Ch 7, p. 190). The engineers were asked to show a "mandatory need" for the very data that would let them decide (Ch 6, p. 157) [AE].

2. <!-- concept: decision-before-analysis --> **Deciding before the analysis.** Before any analysis had started, programme managers had officially shared their belief that the strike was no safety issue, and every manager knew the party line that no safety-of-flight issue was expected (Ch 6, p. 142; Ch 7, p. 181) [AP]. "In both cases, managers' techniques focused on the information that tended to support the expected or desired result at that time" [V] (Ch 8, p. 200).

3. <!-- concept: uncertainty-in-briefings --> **Uncertainty must reach the decider.** "Engineering solutions presented to management should have included a quantifiable range of uncertainty and risk analysis" [V] (Ch 6, p. 168). The assumptions and uncertainty in the Crater analysis "were never fully presented" to the deciding teams, and management focused on the answer rather than the uncertainties [AP] (Ch 6, pp. 145, 160). The analysis also used a model calibrated for objects hundreds of times smaller than the debris (Ch 6, p. 143) [AE].

4. <!-- concept: confirmation-bias --> **The trusted opinion that ends the search.** An expert's early, unanalysed reassurance, from a tile specialist on a question about RCC, settled the matter: "Mission management welcomed this opinion and sought no others." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169). "Managers' tendency to accept opinions that agree with their own dams the flow of effective communications." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169).

5. <!-- concept: minority-opinions --> **Seeking dissent.** "Organizations with strong safety cultures generally acknowledge that a leader's best response to unanimous consent is to play devil's advocate and encourage an exhaustive debate." [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). The Navy's reactor programme holds that when no minority opinions are present, management must do the critical examination itself (Ch 7, p. 183) [AP]. "Imagine the difference if any Shuttle manager had simply asked, "Prove to me that Columbia has not been harmed."" [V] (Ch 7, p. 192).

6. <!-- concept: normalization-of-deviance --> **Drifting risk categories.** Decisions are framed by categories, and NASA's categories drifted: foam went from a safety-of-flight issue to "in family", "accepted risk" and a turnaround issue, and managers confused "accepted risk" with "not a safety-of-flight issue" (Ch 6, pp. 122–130) [AP]. The first acceptance became the precedent, "a precedent for accepting, rather than eliminating, these technical deviations" [V] (Ch 8, p. 196); the Board borrows the name normalisation of deviance from Vaughan [BT].

7. <!-- concept: past-success-as-rationale --> **Past success as a rationale.** The STS-113 flight rationale "is seriously flawed": "With no engineering analysis, Shuttle managers used past success as a justification for future flights" [V] (Ch 6, p. 126). Once accepted, it gave later decision-makers a strong incentive to reuse the same judgement, since arguing otherwise would contradict an established consensus (Ch 6, p. 150) [AP].

8. <!-- concept: consensus-accountability --> **Consensus that diffuses accountability.** The Flight Readiness process, "which is built on consensus verified by signatures of all responsible parties, in effect renders no one accountable" [V]; information was lost at each level for brevity and consensus; and the process transformed "known problems into acceptable flight risks" [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). Safety staff in committee could only choose between "rubber-stamping" and arguing against a side with more information (Ch 7, p. 187) [AP].

9. <!-- concept: schedule-pressure --> **The schedule as a silent decider.** A fixed Node 2 date shaped decisions though management denied undue pressure (Ch 6, p. 131) [AP]. "When a program agrees to spend less money or accelerate a schedule beyond what the engineers and program managers think is reasonable, a small amount of overall risk is added." [V] (Ch 6, p. 139). The Board asks that deadlines be regularly re-evaluated so that any added risk is "recognized, understood, and acceptable" [V] (Ch 6, p. 139).

10. <!-- concept: process-over-merits --> **Process over merits.** Managers asked who was requesting the photos rather than whether they were needed, and imagery requests were cancelled because no one had a "requirement" (Ch 6, pp. 153, 172) [AE]. "Program leaders spent at least as much time making sure hierarchical rules and processes were followed as they did trying to establish why anyone would want a picture of the Orbiter." [V] (Ch 7, p. 181).

11. <!-- concept: different-data-standards --> **Different standards for unprecedented conditions.** In highly uncertain conditions with lives at risk, management failed to recognise "that different data standards — qualitative, subjective, and intuitive — and different processes — democratic rather than protocol and chain of command — were more appropriate" [V] (Ch 8, p. 201). Status set whose evidence counted; "Status mattered. In its absence, numbers were the great equalizer." [V] (Ch 8, p. 202).

12. <!-- concept: independent-technical-authority --> **Separating technical authority from cost and schedule.** The Board's structural answer: the authority to set and waive technical requirements should rest with an independent technical authority, separate from programme managers governed by cost, schedule and mission goals (Ch 7, pp. 184, 193) [AP].

## Questions to Ask During Decision-Making

### Phase 1: Framing (recognising what kind of decision is being made)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Is this inside our experience base? | Is this situation really within past experience, or are we calling it familiar because it resembles something we have seen? | Ch 6, p. 146; Ch 8, p. 200 |
| Which category are we using? | What risk category have we put this in, and has the meaning of that category drifted over time? | Ch 6, pp. 122, 130 |
| Have we decided already? | Did we share a conclusion before any analysis started? | Ch 6, p. 142; Ch 7, p. 181 |
| Is this developmental or routine? | Are we treating an experimental system as if it were operational? | Ch 1, p. 25; Ch 9, p. 208 |

### Phase 2: Bounding (defining the decision space)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Who carries the burden of proof? | Must the option be proved safe, or must the objectors prove it dangerous? | Ch 6, p. 169; Ch 7, p. 190 |
| Has "nothing can be done" been tested? | Have we assumed there are no options without analysing whether there are? | Ch 6, pp. 173–174; Ch 7, p. 181 |
| What is the schedule deciding? | Which commitment or deadline is constraining this choice, and is the risk it adds recognised? | Ch 6, p. 139 |
| Who holds technical authority? | Is the person deciding also the one answerable for cost and schedule? | Ch 7, p. 184 |

### Phase 3: Exploring (generating alternatives)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What information would settle this? | Is there data we could get (imagery, a test, an inspection) that would resolve the question, and who is asking for it? | Ch 6, pp. 140–153 |
| Whose views have we not heard? | Who is marginal to this decision but may know something, and what would it take for them to speak? | Ch 8, p. 203 |
| What did precedent do? | Have we faced this before, and did we then inspect, test or act in a way we are not now? | Ch 6, p. 127 |

### Phase 4: Deciding (analysing and selecting)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What is the uncertainty? | Does the analysis come with a quantified range of uncertainty and its assumptions, and has it been used inside its validated limits? | Ch 6, pp. 143–145, 168 |
| Is the expert expert in this? | Does the trusted opinion cover this question, and who else was asked? | Ch 6, pp. 149, 169 |
| Is agreement too quick? | If the room is unanimous, who is playing devil's advocate? | Ch 7, p. 192 |
| Are we judging merits or channels? | Are we weighing the concern, or whether it came through the proper route? | Ch 6, p. 172; Ch 7, p. 181 |
| Does status decide whose data counts? | Are we demanding numbers from some voices and accepting experience from others? | Ch 8, p. 202 |

### Phase 5: Ratifying (committing to and communicating the decision)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Is someone accountable? | Does sign-off by all parties leave anyone answerable for the risk accepted? | Ch 8, p. 198 |
| Is the rationale fresh? | Are we reusing a rationale accepted before, and does it rest on analysis or on past success? | Ch 6, pp. 126, 150 |
| What did the ratifiers hear? | Did the forum hear the full analysis or a condensed summary? Were the uncertainties on the slide, and where? | Ch 7, pp. 190–192 |
| Did independent safety speak? | Did an independent safety voice review the decision with resources to challenge it? | Ch 7, pp. 186–187 |

### Phase 6: Monitoring (post-decision review)

| Need | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Are we tracking the trend? | Is each recurrence recorded so that a trend can be seen, or only the ones formally classified? | Ch 6, p. 131; Ch 7, p. 189 |
| Is a weak signal being redefined? | When a big surprise arrives, are we analysing it into a weak signal? | Ch 8, p. 197 |
| Is the hazard analysis updated? | When an anomaly occurs, does anything update the hazard analysis behind earlier decisions? | Ch 6, p. 126 |
| Will this vigilance last? | What keeps attention on the risk once the urgency fades? | Ch 9, p. 208 |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| "It's in family" or "we've seen this before" | A familiar-looking event may differ in what matters; the category may have drifted (Ch 6, p. 146; Ch 8, p. 196) | Name the differences from precedent before accepting it |
| A rationale reused from last time | Past success standing in for analysis (Ch 6, p. 126) | Ask what analysis the rationale rests on |
| A concern dismissed as unproven | Inverted burden of proof (Ch 7, p. 190) | Ask for the evidence of safety |
| A decision settled by one reassuring expert | Confirmation; scope of expertise unchecked (Ch 6, p. 169) | Ask what the expert knows about this question, and who else to ask |
| A unanimous room | No devil's advocate; minority views unsought (Ch 7, p. 192) | Assign someone to argue the other side |
| A three-minute summary of a long analysis | Uncertainty dropped as information rose (Ch 7, pp. 190–192) | Ask the analysts for the assumptions and ranges |
| "Who asked for this?" | Process over merits (Ch 6, p. 172) | Judge the request on its content |
| Everyone signed, no one owns it | Consensus diffusing accountability (Ch 8, p. 198) | Name the owner of the accepted risk |

## When to Use This Reference

- **Reach for it** when a group must decide under uncertainty about a potentially serious risk, especially when the decision will be made against a schedule, on the strength of past success, or with a dissenting minority.
- **Reach for it** when designing a recurring readiness or sign-off process, to ask whether it ratifies risk rather than tests it.
- **Pair it** with OpenStax Organizational Behavior or Psychology for general vocabulary on group biases, and with MCDP 1 for decision-making under uncertainty in a different register.
- **Reach for something else** for a well-structured, low-stakes choice among options; the report's lessons concern hazardous decisions.

## Worked Example

The scenario is operator-authored; the report's own case is the loss of Columbia. A hospital trust's executive team must decide whether to go live on a new medication-ordering system on schedule. Testing found three dosage-rounding errors in the past month, each caught by pharmacists and fixed. The supplier says the system is "within tolerance". A clinical-safety officer has asked for a week of parallel running.

**Framing and bounding.** The chair asks the team to say what category the rounding errors are in, and whether that category has shifted: the first was logged as a safety incident, the third as a "known issue" (Source: CAIB, *Report Vol. I*, Ch 6, pp. 122, 130). She asks who must prove what: whether the safety officer must show the system is unsafe, or whether the team must show it is safe to go live (Ch 7, p. 190).

> Organizations that deal with high-risk operations must always have a healthy fear of failure — operations must be proved safe, rather than the other way around. NASA inverted this burden of proof. [V] (Source: Ch 7, p. 190)

**Exploring and deciding.** The supplier's analysis says the errors are rare. The chair asks for the range of uncertainty and the test conditions behind it, and learns that the tests did not cover paediatric doses (Ch 6, pp. 143–145, 168). The IT director's reassurance that "pharmacists will catch it" is checked: pharmacy staffing is reduced on go-live weekend. Because the room is agreeing quickly, the chair asks one director to argue for the delay (Ch 7, p. 192).

> Engineering solutions presented to management should have included a quantifiable range of uncertainty and risk analysis [V] (Source: Ch 6, p. 168)

**Ratifying.** The decision is to run in parallel for one week. The chair records one named owner for the accepted residual risk rather than a list of sign-offs (Ch 8, p. 198).

**Monitoring.** Every rounding error is logged with a trend owner, and the safety officer reports directly to the board on the trend, not through the programme (Ch 6, p. 131; Ch 7, p. 193).

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Deciding before analysing.** Signal: the conclusion circulates before the analysis starts. Diagnosis: the analysis will be read to confirm it (Ch 6, p. 142; Ch 8, p. 200). Follow-up: hold the conclusion until the analysis and its uncertainty are in.
- **Burden reversal.** Signal: objectors told to bring proof. Diagnosis: inverted burden of proof (Ch 7, p. 190). Follow-up: require proof of safety.
- **Familiarity framing.** Signal: "same as last time". Diagnosis: normalisation of deviance (Ch 8, p. 196). Follow-up: compare the actual features.
- **Consensus by signature.** Signal: many sign-offs, no owner. Diagnosis: diffused accountability (Ch 8, p. 198). Follow-up: name the owner.
- **Viewgraph decisions.** Signal: a complex analysis reduced to a slide. Diagnosis: information filtered as it rises (Ch 7, p. 191). Follow-up: read the analysis, not the slide.
- **Schedule as decider.** Signal: every option weighed against a date. Diagnosis: accumulated small risks (Ch 6, p. 139). Follow-up: re-evaluate the date and name the risk it adds.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The normalisation of deviance is credited to Diane Vaughan; the Russian-roulette framing to Feynman; slide analysis to Tufte; high-reliability and normal-accident theory to the scholars the Board consulted. None is held in the corpus; their ideas appear only as the Board reports them.

**Named limits of the source.** The report examines one organisation's decisions about one hazard; it does not set out a general decision method. Its recommendations are for NASA's Human Space Flight Program in 2003. The hospital scenario is the projection's.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every `[V]` and blockquote is copied from the deep reference's verified quotations of the Board's own prose; quoted e-mails, transcripts and outside works are paraphrased.
